title: Legal judgment: Correct output may remain insufficient
desc: Argues automation increases contextual judgment and verification duties while questioning whether assisted performance develops supervisory expertise.

kps.k: The central proposition is that automating legal outputs can increase the importance of contextual judgement without preserving every lawyer task.
kps.d: Legg’s Better than a bot and the 2019 AI-Enhanced Lawyer article distinguish generating predictions or documents from deciding what action serves a client. They anticipate partial substitution, including commoditised services, rather than wholesale lawyer replacement. Their account combines doctrine with experience, empathy, diagnosis and attention to financial and non-financial objectives. The 2019 article’s hypothetical settlement example illustrates why maximising a predicted legal entitlement may conflict with achieving a quicker, more amicable resolution. These arguments draw principally on professional scholarship and conceptual reasoning, not comparative evidence establishing human superiority; the article’s claims about AI’s inability to reason contextually or explain outputs describe its 2019 assessment.

qs.q: There is still a decision to be made about how to use the AI output and what actions to take that will be guided by the larger picture of a client’s objectives.25 The importance of human judgement continues, or even increases, because AI does not per­ form the ‘judgement’ step.
qs.a: Better than a bot – instilling ethical judgement into the lawyers of the future in the age of AI · Academia · 2024

qs.q: 137 While AI may ‘compete with lawyers and undermine their monopoly’ in some areas 138 it will more likely replace some aspects of the lawyer’s role rather than replace lawyers per se.
qs.a: Artificial Intelligence and the Legal Profession: Becoming the AI-Enhanced Lawyer · Academia · 2019

kps.k: Independent judgement and verification impose responsibilities that apparently competent AI output does not discharge.
kps.d: The 2018 Artificially Intelligent Lawyers excerpt argues that blindly passing through ROSS’s analysis may violate Model Rule 2.1 because clients are entitled to their lawyer’s independent assessment. Its time-pressure example is hypothetical, not a finding that all AI use breaches professional duties. The Judgment Premium interprets fabricated-citation court incidents as failures of accountable human verification, while predicting that improved models will only partly resolve hallucinations. Legg adds that judgement must respect duties to justice, clients, independence and integrity, not simply optimise client preferences; client autonomy remains important, but professional limits may require withdrawal.

qs.q: This willingness on the part of the lawyer to circumscribe his efforts and to compromise his thoroughness by offering clients legal advice attained from the blind reliance on technology is not in the best interests of the client and may be considered a violation of Model Rule 2.1 for failing to exercise independent professional judgment.
qs.a: Artificially Intelligent Lawyers: Updating the Model Rules of Professional Conduct in Accordance with the New Technological Era · Academia · 2018

qs.q: The deeper problem those cases reveal is one of abdicated judgment: professionals treating AI output as though it carried the weight of expert analysis, when in fact no one with anything at stake had evaluated whether it was correct.
qs.a: The Judgment Premium · Law firms · 2026

kps.k: The main disagreement concerns whether sound outputs suffice, or whether legal judgement requires something beyond output quality.
kps.d: The Is Law Computable? introduction reports Volokh’s argument that reliably sound opinions could justify accepting AI judges regardless of their internal process. The chapter interprets possible preference for AI judges as resting on an assumption that they avoid human biases, not an established comparison. Sartor and Branting counter that simple rule-chaining and pattern matching cannot adequately model decisions involving contested facts, rules and applications; their objection does not establish that every AI approach must fail. Alarie predicts more data and better pattern recognition over the century while leaving the institutional path uncertain. These positions challenge or qualify the human-judgement thesis, but address judicial decision-making rather than precisely the same duties as client advice.

kps.k: Judgement’s centrality does not establish its uniqueness, infallibility or objective measurability.
kps.d: The supplied institutional-analysis excerpt on Black lawyers cautions that lawyers exaggerate the uniqueness of their judgement while affirming its importance. It argues that contextual discretion makes evaluation of lawyer quality subjective and provisional; the excerpt does not itself establish findings about racial inequality. Legg discusses overconfidence and confirmation bias, while retaining a role for intuition in urgent courtroom decisions. AI-Enhanced Lawyer also acknowledges human fallibility and reports the possibility that statistical analysis could expose hidden biases. These qualifications resist treating professional status alone as evidence of reliable judgement.

qs.q: These two related characteristics render judgments about a lawyer's quality inherently subjective and provi-  sional.
qs.a: Why Are There So Few Black Lawyers in Corporate Law Firms? An Institutional Analysis · Academia · 1996

qs.q: 21 Indeed, one claim made about statistical or machine learning analysis of case law is that it may illuminate the hidden and subconscious biases that influence human decision- makers.
qs.a: Artificial Intelligence and the Legal Profession: Becoming the AI-Enhanced Lawyer · Academia · 2019

kps.k: Better assisted performance does not necessarily develop the expertise needed to supervise AI.
kps.d: Becoming, Doing, Being reports studies in which AI improves weaker performers’ results, but distinguishes those gains from acquiring professional judgement. It argues that experienced lawyers can review outputs effectively only when they understand tool limitations and allocate sufficient review time; juniors may lack the necessary knowledge. The authors leave GenAI’s effects on knowledge acquisition and long-term encoding unresolved. They also warn that AI-based feedback could reduce mentorship and professional contact, while acknowledging variable human supervision. Legg’s concern that automation may remove formative junior tasks therefore identifies a training risk, not a demonstrated outcome.

qs.q: Various studies have shown the capacity for AI and GenAI to lift up the weaker performers in a cohort.
qs.a: Becoming, Doing, Being: GenAI and the Promise of Professional Identity in Law · Academia · 2025

qs.q: How­ ever, this is in a context where AI may replace traditional formative tasks that junior law­ yers learnt from.
qs.a: Better than a bot – instilling ethical judgement into the lawyers of the future in the age of AI · Academia · 2024

kps.k: The proposed response combines experiential learning, reflective supervision and technical literacy.
kps.d: Legg recommends clinics, realistic case studies, simulations, supervised practice and career-long reflection, treating the educational need as longstanding but more urgent under automation. Becoming, Doing, Being emphasises mentoring dialogue that reveals how experienced lawyers handle competing interests and uncertainty. The Judgment Premium recommends consequential work and systematic records of mistakes, supported by personal experience and analogy rather than measured training outcomes. It places greater emphasis on difficult client decisions than routine task execution, while acknowledging that both matter. AI-Enhanced Lawyer adds statistical literacy and management skills to integrate machine predictions with human work.

qs.q: Although the quality of supervision varies, a senior lawyer’s ability to mentor through dialogue, providing insight into how they themselves balance competing interests or make ‘judgement calls’ under uncertainty, is a critical component of the traditional apprenticeship.
qs.a: Becoming, Doing, Being: GenAI and the Promise of Professional Identity in Law · Academia · 2025

qs.q: Develop what you might call an "anti-portfolio": a systematic record of where you were wrong and why.
qs.a: The Judgment Premium · Law firms · 2026

kps.k: A judgement premium remains a conditional economic prediction, not a guarantee of higher fees or access to advice.
kps.d: The Judgment Premium predicts that accountable professional sign-off becomes more valuable as AI-generated work expands. AI-Enhanced Lawyer similarly anticipates greater value for judgement but conditions higher prices on demand and ability to pay. It expects clients to use AI alone when advice costs exceed the stakes or their resources, exposing a tension between the asserted importance of human judgement and access to it. Its practical response includes making lawyers’ contribution more transparent, rather than assuming that professional value automatically translates into affordable services or willingness to pay.

qs.q: The value of that signature will increase, not decrease, as the volume of AI-generated work flowing through it grows, because the need for someone to be accountable scales with the output no one fully authored.
qs.a: The Judgment Premium · Law firms · 2026

qs.q: Greater value can mean a higher price but only if there is demand for lawyer judgement at that price.
qs.a: Artificial Intelligence and the Legal Profession: Becoming the AI-Enhanced Lawyer · Academia · 2019

vlens.an: Across this curated selection of academic and research sources, the principal proposition is generally accepted and materially developed. The common reasoning is that prediction, document generation or other technically competent output does not itself determine what action serves a client or satisfies professional duties: contextual, ethical and independent judgement, together with verification, remains necessary. Several sources extend the proposition by specifying how that capacity should be sustained—through experiential education, reflective practice, technical literacy and mentorship—and by distinguishing immediate AI-assisted performance gains from acquisition of the expertise needed to supervise AI. Material internal variation remains. The institutional-analysis source supports judgement’s centrality while cautioning that it is neither uniquely legal nor objectively measurable; other sources acknowledge human bias and fallibility. Most significantly, the judicial-computability chapter reports a genuine dispute: Volokh’s output-focused view treats reliably sound opinions as potentially sufficient, whereas Sartor and Branting argue that contested adjudication cannot be captured by simple rule-chaining or pattern matching. That judicial debate qualifies, but does not overturn, the broader voice’s development of the proposition; it also concerns adjudication rather than precisely the same professional duties involved in client advice.

qs.q: There is still a decision to be made about how to use the AI output and what actions to take that will be guided by the larger picture of a client’s objectives.25 The importance of human judgement continues, or even increases, because AI does not per­ form the ‘judgement’ step.
qs.a: Better than a bot – instilling ethical judgement into the lawyers of the future in the age of AI · Academia · 2024

qs.q: 197 It may also be effective and efficient for senior lawyers to use GenAI, as they will have sufficient knowledge and experience to adequately judge its outputs,198 provided they understand the limitations of the tool they are using, and take adequate time to review.
qs.a: Becoming, Doing, Being: GenAI and the Promise of Professional Identity in Law · Academia · 2025

vlens.an: This traditional-law-firm source accepts the cluster’s principal proposition that apparently competent AI output does not discharge lawyers’ duties of contextual judgment and verification. It materially extends that proposition in two ways: first, it predicts that expanding AI-generated output will increase the value of accountable professional sign-off; second, it proposes a mechanism for developing supervisory expertise—consequential decision-making combined with systematic reflection on errors. Its reasoning treats fabricated-citation incidents primarily as failures of human verification rather than proof that AI alone is unusable. There is some internal qualification: the source expects better models to reduce hallucinations at least partially, and it acknowledges that routine work builds useful skill, while arguing that high-stakes experience is more important for premium-bearing judgment. The economic “judgment premium” and the developmental benefits of its recommendations remain predictions and experience-based arguments, not measured outcomes. As this facet contains one curated source, its position should not be generalized to traditional law firms as a whole.

qs.q: The deeper problem those cases reveal is one of abdicated judgment: professionals treating AI output as though it carried the weight of expert analysis, when in fact no one with anything at stake had evaluated whether it was correct.
qs.a: The Judgment Premium · Law firms · 2026

qs.q: Judgment comes from decisions with consequences, not from analysis without stakes.
qs.a: The Judgment Premium · Law firms · 2026

elens.an: The pre-2015 source supports the cluster’s foundational proposition that correct or technically competent legal output may be insufficient because effective lawyering also depends on contextual, discretionary judgment. Its reasoning is conceptual: specialised knowledge and technical expertise are necessary, but sound advice and advocacy additionally require experience, insight, interpersonal understanding, cost-benefit assessment and balanced deliberation. The source also supplies an important qualification consistent with the synthesis: judgment is central to good lawyering, but lawyers may exaggerate its uniqueness, and its contextual character makes lawyer quality difficult to assess objectively. Because this period contains only one curated source, no cross-source variation can be inferred; the material variation is within the source’s own account, which affirms judgment while resisting claims that it is uniquely legal or readily measurable. The source does not address automation, AI verification duties, substitution of lawyer tasks, or whether AI-assisted performance develops the expertise required for supervision, so it supports the proposition’s underlying theory rather than its later AI-specific extensions.

qs.q: Good judgment in this context derives from, but ultimately tran-  scends, specialized knowledge and technical expertise.
qs.a: Why Are There So Few Black Lawyers in Corporate Law Firms? An Institutional Analysis · Academia · 1996

elens.an: The 2015–2022 sources support the proposition’s core distinction between producing a legally plausible output and exercising accountable legal judgement. In the lawyering sources, AI is expected to automate predictions and other component tasks rather than replace the contextual, practical and ethical assessment needed to decide what serves a client. They also treat verification as an independent professional responsibility: polished output cannot substitute for a lawyer’s own assessment, particularly where time pressure encourages blind reliance. These claims are primarily conceptual, predictive and doctrinal rather than comparative empirical demonstrations of human superiority. Material internal variation arises in the judicial context. Volokh’s reported position treats reliably sound opinions as potentially sufficient regardless of their production process, directly challenging the proposition, whereas Sartor and Branting argue that simple rule-chaining or pattern matching cannot capture adjudication involving contested facts and rules. Alarie’s forecast of improving data and pattern recognition leaves that dispute unresolved. The period’s sources also propose reskilling and technical literacy, but do not materially examine the cluster’s later concern about whether AI-assisted performance develops the expertise required for effective supervision.

qs.q: The economics approach discussed above suggests that this is because AI separates out human prediction and human judgement, but can only replace prediction, and even then, only under certain conditions.
qs.a: Artificial Intelligence and the Legal Profession: Becoming the AI-Enhanced Lawyer · Academia · 2019

qs.q: 121      In terms of implementing the work of an AI lawyer to a case, when a lawyer relies solely on ROSS’s outputs, independent professional judgment—as required by Model Rule 2.1—vanishes because reliance on such outputs turns into dependence on the judgments of a technological apparatus.
qs.a: Artificially Intelligent Lawyers: Updating the Model Rules of Professional Conduct in Accordance with the New Technological Era · Academia · 2018

elens.an: The sole supplied source for the 2023–2024 generative-shock period accepts the proposition that automated legal output can displace some tasks while increasing the importance of contextual human judgement and verification. Legg materially extends the proposition in two ways. First, he defines the lawyer’s enduring contribution as ethical as well as practical: decisions about how to use AI output must integrate client objectives with duties to justice, independence and integrity, while verification is needed to guard against hallucinations. Second, he develops a concrete training response to the risk that automation removes formative junior work, advocating clinics, realistic case studies, simulations, supervised experience and career-long reflection. His argument is principally conceptual and normative rather than comparative evidence that human judgement is always superior; he also recognises human bias and the possible substitution of AI products for commoditised services.

qs.q: There is still a decision to be made about how to use the AI output and what actions to take that will be guided by the larger picture of a client’s objectives.25 The importance of human judgement continues, or even increases, because AI does not per­ form the ‘judgement’ step.
qs.a: Better than a bot – instilling ethical judgement into the lawyers of the future in the age of AI · Academia · 2024

elens.an: The 2025 source accepts the cluster’s principal proposition that apparently competent GenAI output does not eliminate contextual legal judgement or verification. It materially extends that proposition by distinguishing immediate performance gains from the development of supervisory expertise: senior lawyers may use GenAI effectively when they understand its limitations and devote adequate time to review, whereas junior lawyers may lack the knowledge and experience needed to assess outputs. It also develops the apprenticeship dimension, arguing that situated mentorship helps lawyers learn how to balance competing interests and make judgement calls under uncertainty—capabilities GenAI cannot yet reproduce through output generation or feedback alone. Internal variation lies mainly in degree rather than direction: the source acknowledges that GenAI can improve weaker performers’ results and may benefit experienced lawyers, but treats its effects on knowledge acquisition as unresolved and the possible erosion of mentorship as a risk rather than an established outcome. This assessment concerns the supplied 2025 source and should not be read as representative of all contemporary legal scholarship.

qs.q: 197 It may also be effective and efficient for senior lawyers to use GenAI, as they will have sufficient knowledge and experience to adequately judge its outputs,198 provided they understand the limitations of the tool they are using, and take adequate time to review.
qs.a: Becoming, Doing, Being: GenAI and the Promise of Professional Identity in Law · Academia · 2025

qs.q: Although the quality of supervision varies, a senior lawyer’s ability to mentor through dialogue, providing insight into how they themselves balance competing interests or make ‘judgement calls’ under uncertainty, is a critical component of the traditional apprenticeship.
qs.a: Becoming, Doing, Being: GenAI and the Promise of Professional Identity in Law · Academia · 2025

elens.an: The 2026 source accepts the cluster’s principal proposition that apparently competent AI output remains insufficient without contextual legal judgment and human verification. It materially extends that proposition in two ways: first, it frames accountability for AI-assisted work as the basis of a predicted economic “judgment premium,” because a professional must take responsibility for outputs that no individual fully authored; second, it proposes a mechanism for developing supervisory expertise—exposure to consequential decisions, combined with systematic reflection on errors. The source also distinguishes technical improvement from professional responsibility: better models may partly reduce hallucinations, but cannot remedy lawyers’ abdication of verification and accountable judgment. Its internal qualification is that routine execution still builds useful skill, although the author argues that decisions carrying real stakes are more important for developing premium-bearing judgment. These claims are principally predictions, professional argument, analogy and personal experience rather than measured evidence that this training method improves judgment or that accountable sign-off will command higher fees. As the evidence for this period consists of one curated source, its position should not be treated as representative of 2026 commentary generally.

qs.q: The deeper problem those cases reveal is one of abdicated judgment: professionals treating AI output as though it carried the weight of expert analysis, when in fact no one with anything at stake had evaluated whether it was correct.
